title: Matthew 26:69–75
context: In the courtyard a servant girl, then another, then bystanders confront Peter about being with Jesus. He denies with oath and curse that he does not know the man. The rooster crows; Peter remembers Jesus’ word, goes out, and weeps bitterly.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 26:69–75.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He denied with an oath - To which possibly he was not unaccustomed, before our Lord called him. Surely thou art also one of them, for thy speech discovereth thee - Malchus might have brought a stronger proof than this. But such is the overruling providence of God, that the world, in the height of their zeal, commonly catch hold of the very weakest of all arguments against the children of God.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 26:69–75)

reformed.quote: Here we see that there is no necessity for a severe contest, or for many forces or implements of war, to overpower a man; for any man, who is not supported by the hand of God, will instantly fall by a slight gale or the rustling of a falling leaf. Peter undoubtedly was not less courageous than any of us, and he had already given no ordinary proof of his valor, though it was exercised in a rash and improper manner; and yet he does not wait until he is dragged before the tribunal of the high priest, or until his enemies attempt to put him to death by violence, but, terrified by a woman's voice, immediately denies his Master.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 26:69–75)

verses.text: Now Peter was sitting outside in the court, and a maid came to him, saying, “You were also with Jesus, the Galilean!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Courtyard pressure begins with a servant girl’s observation: you were with Jesus. A small voice brings a large test.

Responsible faith is tried in ordinary conversations, not only in councils. Grace is needed for a clear yes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Peter sits; identification comes. The night Jesus foretold opens with a simple sentence.

Providence uses an unlikely examiner. The word about three denials starts its clock.

verses.text: But he denied it before them all, saying, “I don’t know what you are talking about.”
verses.arminianNotes:
First denial: feigned confusion before them all. Fear edits loyalty in public.

Arminians name this as failure under resistible pressure—Peter could have confessed; he chose evasion. Grace still pursues the denier toward tears.
verses.reformedNotes:
Denial one: I don’t know what you mean. The rock crumbles in speech.

Elect disciples can fall grievously. Christ’s earlier word proves true; Peter’s restoration will also.

verses.text: When he had gone out onto the porch, someone else saw him and said to those who were there, “This man also was with Jesus of Nazareth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He moves to the entrance; another girl tells bystanders. Escape relocates the test; witness spreads.

Changing seats does not remove the call to own Christ. Responsibility follows him.
verses.reformedNotes:
A second person recognizes Peter, this time before a wider audience. Nazareth’s Jesus is named again.

The foretold pattern unfolds step by step. No detail of Jesus’ warning is idle.

verses.text: Again he denied it with an oath, “I don’t know the man.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Denial with an oath, I don’t know the man. Intensity rises; he will not say the Name with belonging.

Oath-backed falsehood compounds sin. Free agency deepens the wound; repentance will need matching depth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Peter denies Jesus with an oath. Peter invokes sacred bond to seal a lie about Jesus.

This is how far self-trust falls. The Lord who predicted it will still look him into life later.

verses.text: After a little while those who stood by came and said to Peter, “Surely you are also one of them, for your speech makes you known.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Accent betrays him—identity leaks when words deny. The bystanders press their certainty.

Creation and history leave marks; pretending neutrality about Jesus often fails. Better truthful confession than thicker cover.
verses.reformedNotes:
Galilean speech exposes him. Providence uses even accent.

The third wave arrives “after a little while,” matching Jesus’ timeline toward the rooster.

verses.text: Then he began to curse and to swear, “I don’t know the man!” Immediately the rooster crowed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Curse and swear: peak denial—then the rooster. Nature itself preaches Jesus’ word.

Arminians hear both Peter’s accountable climax of refusal and mercy in the crowing that stops the spiral. The sign is grace interrupting, not mere humiliation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Self-curse, oath, denial—then immediate crow. Prophecy punctuates the night.

Jesus’ “truly” stands. The rooster is the Lord’s appointed messenger to Peter’s conscience.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the denials as sin and the rooster as mercy-tinged fulfillment. Arminians typically stress Peter’s free, deepening failure and grace that interrupts toward repentance; Calvinists underline Christ’s sure word coming to pass and the keeping purpose that will restore this disciple.

verses.text: Peter remembered the word which Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Then he went out and wept bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes:
Memory of Jesus’ saying, then bitter tears. Repentance begins where the Lord’s word lands on a broken heart.

Weeping is not the end—Galilee still waits. Grace that enables later restoration already works in godly sorrow. No straw man of cheap tears; this is grief over denying the Lord.
verses.reformedNotes:
He remembers Jesus’ saying—then goes out weeping bitterly. The word does the wounding and the beginning of healing.

Bitter tears under Christ’s true word are the path home. The Shepherd who foresaw the denials also foresaw this grief and the breakfast of restoration still to come.
